newsitem.title: ZAIRE: New Zaire notes released amid controversy.
newsitem.headline: New Zaire notes released amid controversy.

text.p: The Central Bank in Zaire began releasing new larger denomination bank notes this week with critics rejecting the move as inflationary.
"We have supplied the banks with instructions for them to release the money gradually," Victor Mwazaka, director of the monetary department of the Central Bank told Reuters.
Zaire's civil servants, many of whom have not received their meagre salaries for months, would be paid with the new notes, he added.
Mwazaka said that over the weekend the new zaire had tumbled in anticipation of the release of the new bills but that the bank had intervened to bolster the currency.
"We have intervened with $2 million to support the currency," he said, referring to purchases of new zaires from commercial banks.
An initial batch of the bills, with face values of 100,000, 500,000 and one million new zaires, were printed in Germany, for release to commercial banks on Monday.
Mwazaka said the state copper giant, Gecamines, financed the printing of the bills.
Since the announcement last Friday that the new bills would be circulated, the new zaire has slumped against the U.S. dollar, and the prices of basic commodities have shot up.
On Tuesday the new zaire was selling at 165,000 to the dollar on the informal market, compared to 120,000 last week.
The price of a sack of manioc has gone from three million zaires to five million in a less than a week.
The bank justifies the printing of the notes saying that they keep up with inflation, and will be easier to carry than stackloads of denominations worth less than 50 U.S. cents.

Critics say the new notes fuel inflation -- measured in October at a year-on-year rate of 681 percent -- and that an average civil servant with a salary equivalent to less than a dollar a month, cannot even earn the largest denomination note in a year.
"It will have catastrophic consequences both for the population and for economic operators," Bemba Saolona, the president of the Zairean business association, ANEZA, said.

Bemba, once President Mobutu Sese Seko's personal financial manager, predicted petrol prices would surge and businesses collapse, while basic commodities, including medicines, would climb beyond the reach of Zaire's already impoverished people.
Members of the radical opposition allied to Etienne Tshisekedi, which commands huge popularity among Kinshasa's poorer inhabitants, on Saturday urged a boycott of the notes.
Zaire is in the throes of a major political crisis, with a major rebellion in its eastern lands.

The issue of new bank notes during a period of galloping inflation in 1992 led to widespread looting by soldiers after the radical opposition rejected the bills as worthless pieces of paper. Soldiers were paid in the new bills.
